newsitem.title: GREECE: Greek seamen extend crippling nine-day strike.
newsitem.headline: Greek seamen extend crippling nine-day strike.

text.p: Striking Greek seamen on Tuesday extended a nine-day walkout that has left dozens of trucks stranded at ports and threatened remote Greek islands with food and fuel shortages.
The strike to press for better pensions, insurance and tax treatment affects all ships with Greek crews and has kept most vessels idle at ports around the country.

Labour groups have reacted strongly to Greece's 1997 budget, described as the toughest in 15 years, but technocrat Prime Minister Costas Simitis says bitter medicine is necessary for the country and has rejected all union demands.
The Panhellenic Seamen's Federation (PNO) decided to extend their strike, due to end on Tuesday, until Thursday.
"We have no indications that our problems will be resolved," PNO representative George Maroulakis told an Athens daily. "We have no other path to take."

Scores of trucks have been lined up waiting for ferries to sail, tonnes of farm produce has been rotting at ports and remote Greek islands dependent on ships for survival have reported the first shortages in medicine, food and supplies.
"Life is difficult for us in the winter without a boat," the mayor of the Aegean island of Sikinos told an Athens daily. "If we run out of medicine it will be tragic."

Scuffles have broken out between seamen, angry farmers and truck drivers at the ports of Piraeus, the Peloponnese and on the island of Crete. Special coast guard forces have intervened to keep them apart.

Exporters on the island of Crete said damage to the island's economy had reached $68 million and was rising. The defence ministry has sent air carriers and navy vessels to Crete to transport perishables destined for export.
PNO has defied a court ruling on Friday declaring their strike illegal, risking fines and arrests.

"Everyone must respect justice. There is a limit to everything," government spokesman Dimitris Reppas told reporters. "Government policy is not formed according to the demands of a special interest group."
The socialist goverment, elected in September, successfully waited out a crippling farmers' blockade in December but is facing a new wave of strikes against its tough budget and incomes policy.

High school teachers began an indefinite strike to press for better pay on Monday while Greece's biggest labour confederation, GSEE, has announced a 24-hour nationwide walkout against a new tax system for Thursday.
The GSEE strike is expected to disrupt transport, state hospitals and public services. A number of state companies will be forced to operate with skeleton staffs.
Farmers have also threatened to repeat their paralysing road blockade if they get no government pledges by February 4 that their demands for higher price supports, fuel and tax cuts will be met.
